newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Analysts see forestry volatile rest of 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Analysts see forestry volatile rest of 1997.

text.p: The Nordic forestry industry is in for a bumpy ride for the rest of 1997, with pulp prices expected to tumble by the year end and advertised fine paper price rises not materialising, analysts said on Thursday.

Although reports from Sweden and Finland's major forestry companies for the first half of 1997 tried to paint a mildly positive outlook for the third and fourth quarters, analysts the sector was unlikely to see any pick-up.

All of the main players, ending with Sweden's MoDo and Finland's UPM-Kymmene on Thursday, said the first half was characterised by high volumes and low prices but prices would recover in the second half. Companies were coy about longer-term forecasts.
"I think that most companies are being too optimistic when it comes to prices," said analyst Claes Vikbladh from Nordiska Fondkommission.
"This is a non-inflationary environment where it is very difficult to push up prices to consumers, especially as there are not really any demand/supply problems in the sector."
Analyst Denis Christie from Dresdner Kleinwort Benson told Reuters that the sector would remain volatile, and this had a lot to do with pulp prices.

"As pulp prices are raised, production will be raised as well and I think pulp prices will drop by the end of the third quarter, making other product prices weaker," said Christie, adding that pulp prices could fall as low as $500-550 per tonne by year end.
"I think there is a lot of 'hope value' that will not come to fruition in the next six months. We have seen quite a good run this week and this could be the end of it now."

Several pulp producers in the U.S. and the Nordic region have announced plans to raise prices to around $610 per tonne from $580, while fine paper producers are expected to increase prices by about eight to 12 percent from September 1.

But analysts said there was a risk that paper manufacturers would not be able to recoup the higher cost of pulp, and would introduce production stoppages which could lead to a fall in pulp shipments and a build up in stocks.
Stock levels are already starting to rise above shipment levels, one analyst noted.

The pulp futures market, Pulpex, currently prices pulp at $560 a tonne for late September, the end of the seasonally weak third quarter. Real prices include transportation and are usually negotiated at a discount of between five and ten percent.
The current strength of the U.S. dollar was also seen affecting the sector's performance.
The firm dollar prevents North American producers from selling newsprint or kraftliner into Europe, giving European producers an upper hand and possible price strength.
Analysts were sceptical that many of the price rises would happen.
"There is quite a high risk that some of the increases that have been announced might not go through," said Christie.
Vikbladh said excess capacity would make it hard to raise pulp prices above $600 per tonne.
"It would be more or less impossible to raise prices to consumers and that makes it hard to raise the price of the raw commodity," Vikbladh said.
"Demand will improve and volumes will get better in the second half but we don't expect prices to rise and price is what moves profits the most in these companies."
